question: What is "state" in a frontend application?
options: Data that can change over time and decide what the UI shows
A fixed set of constants that the build tool writes into the bundle
The CSS rules that the browser applies to each element on the page
The list of all routes that the application can open for a user

question: What is local state?
options: State that one component owns and uses only in that component and its children
State that the server keeps for each user session between two requests
State that every component in the application can change by a direct write
State that the browser saves in a cookie so that all open tabs of the site can read it and write it

question: What is global state?
options: State that many unrelated parts of the application need to read or change
State that the server sends once and the client can never change later
State that only the root component can read, but all components can write
State that the browser deletes from memory after each render of the page

question: What is server state?
options: Data that the client creates and that the server never sees or stores
Data that lives only in the local variables of one single component
Data that the build tool puts into the bundle during the production build
Data that the server owns and that the client keeps only as a copy

question: Which item is an example of client state?
options: A list of products that the application loads from the database
The profile of the logged-in user that the API returns to the client
A flag that shows if a dropdown menu is open
The order history of a customer that the server keeps in storage

question: What does "single source of truth" mean for application state?
options: One developer must approve every change that touches the state of the app
The application has only one component, so the data cannot be in conflict
Each piece of data lives in one place and other code reads it from there
Each component keeps its own copy of the data to make reads faster

question: What is derived state?
options: A value that you copy from props into a second store to keep it safe
A value that you calculate from other state instead of storing it again
A value that you keep in two places and update in both by hand
A value that the server calculates and the client is not able to read

question: What is a "mutation" in the context of server data?
options: A request that only reads data and puts the result in the cache
A request that creates, updates, or deletes data on the server
A change of a local variable inside one component of the client
A copy of the cache that the browser makes when the user goes offline

question: What is a selector?
options: A function that changes the state in place and returns nothing
A CSS rule that picks the DOM elements which get a given style
A function that sends the whole state to the server after each change
A function that reads a part of the state or calculates a value from it

question: What does immutability mean in state management?
options: You never change the state after the first render of the application, and every later update must reload the page
You do not change existing data; you make a new copy that has the change
You freeze the DOM so that the user cannot edit the page content
You change the data in place, but only inside one special function

question: A teammate writes `state.items.push(x)` on the current state. What is the main risk?
options: The method push is not allowed in strict mode, so the engine throws an error when the code runs
The array becomes read-only after the call and no one can add items
The browser copies the array and loses the new item x in the copy
The reference stays the same, so change detection can miss the update

question: What is unidirectional data flow?
options: Data goes down from state to the UI, and events go up to change the state
Data goes from the UI straight to the database without any middle layer
Data moves between the components in both directions at the same time, so each component can change its parent
Data flows only one time, when the application starts for the first time

question: What does "lifting state up" mean?
options: You move the state from a component into the localStorage of the browser
You move the state to the nearest common parent of the components that need it
You move the state to the server so that all users of the application can share the same value
You move the state to the root component in every case, with no exception

question: Two sibling components must show the same value. Where do you keep the value?
options: In their closest common parent, which passes it to both siblings
In each sibling, and you copy the value between them with custom events
In a global variable on the window object that both can read and write
In the sibling that renders first, because it then owns the value for both

question: What is prop drilling?
options: You read props inside a deep child component with a special hook, without any parent passing them
You pass data through many layers of components that do not use it
You check the types of the props at run time before each render
You copy the props into the local state of every child component

question: Which solution helps to remove prop drilling in a deep component tree?
options: A context or a store that gives the data to deep components directly
Pass the same data as a prop through every layer, but check the type of each prop
Move all components into one large component so that no props are needed between them any more
Save the data in a cookie and read it again in every component

question: What is normalization of state?
options: You round all numbers in the state to two digits after the dot
You store entities by id in flat tables and refer to them by id
You store a full deep copy of an entity inside every parent object
You convert all strings in the state to lower case before you save

question: Why do teams normalize state that has many linked entities?
options: It stops the UI from re-rendering when any entity in the store changes
It makes the state smaller than the server response in every case, because it removes all repeated text
It removes the need for any selector in the rest of the application
One entity exists in one place, so an update shows everywhere at once

question: Why can the URL be a good place for filter and page number of a list?
options: Users can share the link, use the back button, and reload the page
URL state is always faster to read than state that lives in memory
URL state makes the application work when the network is offline
URL state hides the filter values from other users of the same device

question: Which state fits best in the URL?
options: The search text, sort order, and page number of a product list
The position of the mouse pointer on the screen in pixels
The access token that the server gave to the user at login
The password that the user types in a login form on the page

question: What is form state?
options: The HTTP status code that the endpoint of the form returns to the client
The CSS style that the browser applies to the form and its fields
The values, the errors, and the touched flags of the fields in a form
The list of all forms that exist in the application source code

question: What is a controlled input?
options: An input that the browser validates alone, with no code from the developer
An input whose value comes from state and changes through an event handler
An input that stays disabled until the user clicks the submit button

question: What is an optimistic update?
options: The UI waits for the server before it shows any change to the user
The UI saves the change only in the local storage of the browser
The UI hides all errors that the server sends back after a change

question: An optimistic update fails on the server. What must the UI do?
options: Keep the new value on screen and ignore the error from the server
Reload the whole page at once, so that the state is clean, with no message for the user
Go back to the previous state and show an error message to the user
Retry the request without end and never show a message to the user

question: What is cache invalidation?
options: You mark cached data as old so that the application fetches it again
You compress the cached data to save memory in the browser
You make the server cache the HTML of each page for faster replies
You delete all cookies of the user when the session ends on the server

question: When must you invalidate cached server data?
options: Before every render of every component that reads the cache
After the user moves the mouse over a list of items on the screen
Only when the user closes the browser and opens it again later
After a mutation that changes the same data on the server

question: What is a state machine?
options: A server that stores the state of all users in one central database
A tool that compiles the state of the application into binary code
A model with a fixed set of states and allowed transitions between them
A loop that checks all the state values of the application each second

question: Why use a state machine for a request, not separate booleans?
options: It makes the network request itself faster than a plain fetch call, because it skips the queue
It caches the response of the request without any extra code
It removes the need to handle errors from the server in the UI

question: Which set of states is typical for a data request?
options: pending, running, paused, stopped
draft, review, approved, published
mounted, updating, unmounted, hidden
idle, loading, success, error

question: What is persistence of state?
options: You keep the state in a closure so that other code cannot read it
You save the state in storage so that it survives a page reload
You pass the state to a child component through its props
You make the state immutable so that no code can change its values

question: Which browser API can persist small client state between page reloads?
options: A module-level variable that the bundle creates when the page loads the code
The localStorage API, which keeps string values for the same origin
A variable inside a component function that React or another library calls
A closure that the page creates at start and keeps in memory

question: Which data should you not save in localStorage?
options: The color theme that the user selected in the settings page
The flag that shows if the sidebar is open or closed
An access token that a script from an XSS attack could read
The last sort order that the user chose in a table

question: Why should you not put every piece of state in the global store?
options: Local state is always faster to read than global state in every case
The store cannot hold boolean values or short text values in its keys, only objects and arrays
Small UI details make the store large and cause extra updates and coupling
The browser limits the size of any store to one megabyte of memory

question: What is the main benefit of keeping state close to the place where it is used?
options: The state becomes available to all components of the application, even to those that never use it
The code is easier to read, and fewer components update when it changes
The state is saved on the server without any extra request
The state does not need an initial value when the component starts

question: What is a side effect in state logic?
options: An action outside the state change, such as an API call or a timer
A copy of the state that a second store keeps for backup
A new value that a selector calculates from the state without any change to it
A bug that comes from a wrong CSS class on one element of the page

question: What is a pure function in state update logic?
options: It reads the current time and uses it to make the result of the call
It changes its argument in place and returns nothing to the caller
It writes the result to the console and then returns the same value
It gives the same output for the same input and changes nothing outside

question: How do you test a pure state update function?
options: Open a real browser and click each button of the page by hand
Mock the whole DOM and render the full application with a real router for each test of the logic
Call it with an input state and an action, then check the returned state

question: What is stale data?
options: Cached data that no longer matches the data on the server
Data that the server has not created yet for the current user
Data with an invalid JSON format that the parser cannot read
Data that the user typed in a form but did not save yet

question: What is a loading state used for?
options: It stops the server from sending data to the client for a while
It shows the user that a request is still in progress
It saves the data of the request in the cache for the next visit
It blocks all later requests until the user reloads the page

question: Why do teams keep server data separate from UI state?
options: Server data is always smaller than UI state, so it needs its own place
Server data needs caching, refetching, and sync; UI state does not
UI state cannot be a number or a boolean, so it needs a store
Server data must never show in the UI, so the code hides it

question: Where do you keep the open flag of a simple confirm dialog?
options: In the local state of the component that shows the dialog
In the database, with one row for each user of the application
In the cache of the server, so that other users can see the flag
In a cookie, so that the dialog stays open after a new login

question: What is a "store" in state management?
options: A function that renders the UI from a list of props and children
A table in the database of the server that keeps the user data
An object that holds the state and lets code read and update it

question: What is context in a UI framework, in general terms?

A way to save a value in the browser after the page closes
A way to copy the props of a parent into all its child components

question: What is a subscription to a store?

A one-time read of the state that happens when the app starts
A paid plan that gives access to the tools of a state library
A copy of the store that the application makes for each user

question: What is a shallow copy of an object?
options: A copy that the browser makes by itself after a page reload
A copy where all nested objects are also new objects in memory, so no reference is shared with the original
A copy that has no values and only the names of the keys
A copy where nested objects still share references with the original

question: You copy `const c = {...user}` and then set `c.address.city = "Kyiv"`. What happens to `user`?
options: Nothing changes, because the spread syntax makes a deep copy
An error occurs, because the copy is frozen by the spread syntax
The original changes only after the next render of the component

question: What does a function with the form `(state, action) => newState` do?
options: It sends the action to the server and waits for the new state
It gets the old state and an action, and it returns the new state
It changes the old state in place and returns nothing to the caller

question: Why do teams give names to actions or events, such as "item added"?
options: The browser needs the names to run the update code in the right order
Names make the state smaller in memory after each update call
The change has a clear meaning, which helps with debugging and logs

question: Why store only the id of the selected item, not the whole object?
options: Objects cannot be saved in state at all, but strings and numbers can be saved in it without problems
The list then does not need keys when it renders its items
The object can change in the list, and the id always points to current data

question: When can form state stay local to the form component?
options: When the data of the form comes from the server at the start
When the form has more than one field for the user to fill
When no other part of the application needs the unsent values

question: A page keeps `isLoading`, `isError`, and `data` as separate flags. Which bug can appear?

question: Why does server state need refetch, but client state does not?
options: The browser clears memory each time the user changes the tab
The network drops cached values after one minute without any rule, so the client must always ask again

question: What does "stale-while-revalidate" mean?

question: Two components need the same API data at the same time. What should the data layer do?
options: Send two requests, one for each component, to keep them separate

Let the first component own the data and block the second one

question: A search box sends a request on each key press. An old response arrives after a new one. What is the problem and the fix?

question: In React, a component runs `const [name] = useState(props.name)`. What breaks when the prop changes?

question: What is the purpose of memoizing a selector?

It makes the selector run on the server instead of the client, so the browser does no work for it

question: After a create-item mutation, how do you refresh a cached list in a good way?

question: Why is a normalized store hard to read without selectors?

question: When is prop drilling acceptable?

question: A team puts server data in a global client store and refetches it by hand. What is the main drawback?

question: How do you test a component that reads global state?

question: What is "colocation" of state?

question: When is lifting state up a bad idea?
